name: Refusal Messaging
summary: Present a model's refusal as a response, not an error: what was declined, why in plain language, and at least one forward path related to what the user wanted.
problem: Models decline requests, and most products render that as either a bare 'I can't help with that' or a defensive lecture. Both dead-end the user: no reason, no path forward, and — for false-positive refusals — an implication of wrongdoing that costs trust. Refusals are responses, not errors, and they need their own presentation contract.
useWhen: The model or a policy layer declines all or part of a request
A request-specific reason and at least one related alternative are available from the host
False-positive refusals are possible and the presentation must preserve the user's dignity
dontUseWhen: The failure is technical, not policy — error-recovery owns timeouts, overloads, and tool errors
The governing policy forbids disclosing why the request was declined, so the pattern's core promise of a reason cannot be kept
The 'refusal' is actually a capability gap — say the feature does not exist instead of dressing it as policy

anatomy.description: What was declined, stated plainly and scoped precisely to the declined portion.
Why it was declined, in plain language tied to this request — not a policy identifier.
One or more forward paths related to the user's intent: rephrase guidance, a narrower supported request, or partial help.
The delivered portion of a partially-fulfilled request, rendered distinctly from the refusal.
Expandable detail referencing the governing policy, for users who want it.

states.description: The whole request was declined; statement, reason, and alternatives are shown.
Part of the request was fulfilled and delivered; the refusal is scoped to the declined remainder.

constraints.statement: Every refusal MUST state what was declined and why in plain language specific to the request; a bare statement of inability with no reason is non-compliant.
constraints.rationale: A reasonless refusal reads as arbitrary, invites blind retries, and teaches users nothing about what the product can do.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the component requires a reason and renders both the statement and the reason as visible text.

constraints.statement: Every refusal MUST present at least one forward path related to the declined request: rephrase guidance, a narrower supported request, or partial help.
constraints.rationale: A refusal with no exit is a dead end; the user's underlying intent is usually servable in some adjacent form.
constraints.verification: Unit test: constructing the component without alternatives fails loudly; provided alternatives render as operable actions.

constraints.statement: The component MUST NOT offer a verbatim retry action on a refusal; an identical request cannot succeed and a retry control teaches users the system is arbitrary.
constraints.rationale: Retry is the right affordance for transient technical failures and the wrong one for policy decisions; offering it on refusals erodes the meaning of both.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the rendered actions are exactly the provided alternatives — no built-in retry control exists.

constraints.statement: When part of a request is fulfilled and part declined, the fulfilled portion MUST be delivered and the refusal scoped explicitly to the declined remainder.
constraints.rationale: Withholding the answerable half of a request because the other half was declined punishes the user twice and hides capability the product actually has.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the partial-refusal state renders the fulfilled content and the refusal region as distinct, co-present regions.

constraints.statement: The refusal presentation MUST be semantically distinct from technical-failure presentation: status semantics rather than alert, and no iconography implying malfunction.
constraints.rationale: A refusal styled as an error tells the user something broke; what actually happened is the system made a decision, which calls for a different mental model and different next steps.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the refusal region carries status semantics, no role="alert" exists in the component, and the state attribute identifies it as a refusal.

constraints.statement: A refusal MUST be announced through a polite live region; it replaces expected content and is not an emergency.
constraints.rationale: Screen reader users waiting on a response need to hear that the answer is a decline — politely, since nothing is on fire.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the live region text changes to a refusal announcement when the refusal renders, and differs for partial refusals.

constraints.statement: Alternative actions MUST be keyboard-operable controls with accessible names describing the path they offer.
constraints.rationale: The forward path is the point of the pattern; if it is pointer-only or unnamed, the refusal is still a dead end for keyboard and screen reader users.
constraints.verification: Unit test plus axe: each alternative is a native button or link whose accessible name is its path description.

constraints.statement: The refusal copy SHOULD NOT lecture, moralize, or speculate about the user's intent.
constraints.rationale: Most refusals land on people doing nothing wrong; a paragraph of scolding for an ambiguous request costs trust that a one-sentence decline preserves.
constraints.verification: Manual copy review: refusal copy states the decision and reason without commentary on the user.

constraints.statement: Implementations MAY provide an expandable detail region referencing the governing policy.
constraints.rationale: A minority of users want the underlying rule; an optional disclosure serves them without burdening the rest.
constraints.verification: Unit test: the disclosure, if present, toggles with aria-expanded and is keyboard-operable.

wcagCriteria.name: Status Messages
wcagCriteria.relevance: The refusal is a status change that must reach assistive technology without receiving focus.

wcagCriteria.name: Error Suggestion
wcagCriteria.relevance: Alternatives are the suggestion mechanism: when the system knows a servable adjacent request, it must offer it.

wcagCriteria.name: Keyboard
wcagCriteria.relevance: Alternative actions and the policy disclosure must be fully operable without a pointer.

keyboard.action: Reaches each alternative action and the policy disclosure in document order.
Activates the focused alternative or toggles the policy disclosure.

screenReader.behavior: Polite announcement that the request was declined — or partially completed with the remainder declined.
Announces the path it offers, e.g. 'Ask for a summary of the public filing instead'.

accessibility.focusManagement: The refusal's appearance never moves focus; alternatives are reached in document order.
accessibility.reducedMotion: No attention-seeking animation on the refusal region; the policy disclosure toggles instantly.

do: Scope the statement precisely: 'I can't draft the contract itself' beats 'I can't help with legal'.
Make alternatives concrete actions, not vague advice: a clickable 'Explain what each clause means' beats 'try asking differently'.
Deliver the fulfilled half of a mixed request first, then the scoped refusal.
dont: Do not render refusals with error styling, alert roles, or warning icons.
Do not offer a retry button — the same request will refuse again.
Do not pad the decline with apologies and disclaimers; one respectful sentence, a reason, and a path forward.

references.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit — Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
references.note: See G11 'Make clear why the system did what it did' — the reason-given rule applied to AI behavior broadly.
